transcript.content: Hello, I'm Dr. Smith. It's nice to meet you; could you tell me what brings you in to see me today?

Nice to meet you, Dr. Smith. Well, I'm here because... I've just been having these thoughts lately. I keep thinking that my family might be better off if I just didn't wake up. 

It really scared me, honestly. It bothered me enough that I ended up telling my supervisor at work about it, and... well, that's what pushed me to finally come in and see you today.
Have you ever felt this way before, perhaps months or years ago, or is this the very first time you have experienced these kinds of feelings?

Well, looking back on it... I guess these low stretches have been coming around for about a year now. So, no, it's not the very first time I've felt down. But this time around... especially after my daughter left... it's just hit me the hardest. I haven't had it get quite this bad before.
During the past year, have there been any periods of a few months or longer where you felt completely like your normal self, or has your mood been consistently low this entire time?

You know, I haven't really kept track of it like that. I'm not entirely sure. 

I don't think it's been consistently low every single day, but... as for having a solid few months where I felt completely back to normal, I really couldn't say. When I try to look back over the whole year, it all just kind of runs together. I just know it's been coming and going.
During these times when you feel low, do you find that you lose interest or pleasure in almost all of your usual activities?

Yeah, I really do. I used to... well, I used to mess with my tomato plants a lot, or I'd be out sanding wood at my work bench. I'd watch the Falcons play, and I'd always stay after church just talking with folks. But lately... I don't know. I just look at all that stuff now like it belongs to somebody else. I just don't have the drive to do any of it right now.
During these past few months when you've felt your lowest, have there been specific weeks where your appetite, sleep, or energy levels were drastically different than your usual self?

Well, as far as my appetite goes, yeah, it's been pretty different. Most days I really just have to make myself eat a few bites. Even the food I normally like, whether I'm at the warehouse or at home... it just sits there. I usually end up throwing it out because I just can't bring myself to eat it.
Looking back over the past year, can you recall any specific stretches of two months or longer where you felt completely like your usual self, without these low feelings?

Like I was saying a little bit ago, I really just don't know for sure. Two whole months is a long time, and... well, I don't think I've had a stretch that long where I felt completely normal. I haven't marked it down on a calendar or anything, but no, I can't recall a specific time like that where the low feelings were just completely gone.

During these periods when you feel your lowest, have you ever noticed that you have trouble concentrating or making simple decisions, or have you felt unusually restless or slowed down in your movements?

Yeah, the concentration part... that's definitely a struggle. When I'm down at the distribution center, I'll just sit there and stare at the schedule or the routing sheet, and my mind just won't lock in on it. Because of that, making even simple decisions gets tough. Like, little staffing calls about who needs to be where—they end up feeling way bigger and harder to figure out than they ought to.

You mentioned these low feelings have been coming and going for about a year now; before that year began, did you have a period of at least a year or more where you felt consistently like your normal self?

Before this past year? Hmm. You know, I really couldn't say for sure. I mean, I don't remember feeling this bad back then, but I also don't remember if I had a whole year where I felt completely fine, either. It's just hard to think back that far and know exactly how I was feeling day to day.

Looking back over your life, have there ever been any periods lasting at least a few days where you felt unusually energetic, talkative, or productive, to the point where you felt like you didn't need much sleep?

Yeah, I have. There was a stretch for a while where I just had so much energy. I'd be awake and up way before daylight, just... planning out changes for the warehouse. And then I'd be at home cleaning out the entire garage. I was just jumping from one job right to the next, and honestly, I really didn't even want to stop.
During that time when you had all that extra energy and were getting so much done, did it ever reach a point where it caused real trouble for you at work or with the people in your life?

No, I wouldn't say it caused any real trouble. Honestly, I was getting a lot done at work, and my wife was just happy the garage finally got cleaned out. I didn't get into any arguments or make any bad decisions that messed anything up. I just felt really good and got a lot accomplished.
Thinking back to that time when you had all that extra energy and were getting so much done, about how many days in a row did that feeling last?

Well... I couldn't really give you an exact number. I wasn't counting the days or anything like that. It was just a good stretch of time. I just remember feeling that way for a bit before things eventually settled back down, but I'm not sure exactly how many days in a row it was.
When you had that stretch of extra energy where you were cleaning the garage and working on warehouse plans, was that feeling of being 'up' something that lasted for at least four days in a row?

I really couldn't tell you for sure. It might have been four days, or maybe a little more, or even a little less. Like I was saying, I wasn't marking it on a calendar. I just remember it being a solid stretch of time where I was going non-stop and feeling good. But as far as knowing if it hit exactly four days in a row... I just don't know.
During that time when you had all that extra energy and were getting so much done, did your wife or colleagues ever comment that you were acting differently than your usual self?

Well, my wife did say something. She mentioned I was talking a lot faster than normal and that I just seemed really... wired, I guess. At work, one of the guys asked what I had in my coffee because I was moving so fast and getting all those plans drawn up so quickly. So yeah, people definitely noticed I was acting different than my usual self.

During that time when you were feeling so 'wired' and energetic, was the change in your behavior or mood ever significant enough that you had to be hospitalized or see a doctor specifically for that 'up' feeling?

No, no, nothing like that. I didn't go to a hospital or even see a doctor about it. I just thought I was having a really productive couple of days, you know? It didn't seem like something I needed to get checked out for.
Looking back further than just this past year, can you recall a period of time before that when you felt consistently down or depressed for a year or more?

I don't think so, no. I mean, I've had times where I felt down, sure, but... not for a whole year straight. Not that I can remember, anyway. It's usually just a few weeks or maybe a month or two where things feel really heavy, but it hasn't ever dragged on for a full year or more before this recent stuff.
Looking back at that time when you felt so energetic and wired, did that period ever last for a full week or longer?
No, it didn't last that long. It was just a few days, maybe four or five at the most, where I felt like that. It definitely wasn't a whole week.

There is no specific symptom profile item for 'observable by others' or 'change in functioning uncharacteristic of the individual' (Criterion C and D of hypomania) other than the manifestations already provided in the symptom items themselves, but none explicitly address the question of whether others noticed the change overall.

patient.answer: Well, my wife did say something. She mentioned I was talking a lot faster than normal and that I just seemed really... wired, I guess. At work, one of the guys asked what I had in my coffee because I was moving so fast and getting all those plans drawn up so quickly. So yeah, people definitely noticed I was acting different than my usual self.

inference.note: The patient's report of a distinct period of elevated energy, increased talkativeness, and 'wired' behavior, which was noticeable to others, suggests a hypomanic episode. F34.1 (Dysthymia) is less likely given the severity of the current depressive episode (suicidal ideation, significant functional impairment), shifting the focus toward a Bipolar spectrum disorder.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's period of elevated mood and energy was severe enough to require hospitalization, which would distinguish between Bipolar I (F31.0) and other mood disorders.
doctor.question: During that time when you were feeling so 'wired' and energetic, was the change in your behavior or mood ever significant enough that you had to be hospitalized or see a doctor specifically for that 'up' feeling?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if the manic/hypomanic episode resulted in hospitalization, which is a criterion for distinguishing mania from hypomania, but there is no specific symptom in the profile for hospitalization or severity of the elevated episode.

patient.answer: No, no, nothing like that. I didn't go to a hospital or even see a doctor about it. I just thought I was having a really productive couple of days, you know? It didn't seem like something I needed to get checked out for.

doctor.intent: To determine if the patient experienced these periods of low mood (dysthymia) for at least two years, which is required for a diagnosis of F34.0 (Persistent Depressive Disorder).
doctor.question: Looking back further than just this past year, can you recall a period of time before that when you felt consistently down or depressed for a year or more?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about a history of feeling consistently down or depressed for a year or more prior to the past year (exploring criteria for dysthymia/persistent depressive disorder or a longer history of depression). The symptom profile contains 'depressive_episode_duration' which states 'Looking back, the low stretches have been coming around for about a year...', but does not cover a period *before* that past year lasting for a year or more. Therefore, there is no specific item for a depression duration longer than the 1 year mentioned.

patient.answer: I don't think so, no. I mean, I've had times where I felt down, sure, but... not for a whole year straight. Not that I can remember, anyway. It's usually just a few weeks or maybe a month or two where things feel really heavy, but it hasn't ever dragged on for a full year or more before this recent stuff.

inference.note: The patient's report of a period of elevated mood (hypomania) that was noticeable to others but did not require hospitalization or cause severe impairment, combined with the current depressive episode, makes Bipolar II disorder (F31.8) or Bipolar I, current episode hypomanic (F31.0) more likely than Persistent Depressive Disorder (F34.0). F34.0 is less likely given the lack of a clear two-year history of chronic low mood prior to the current year.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient has experienced a full manic episode (at least 7 days or requiring hospitalization) to distinguish between Bipolar I and Bipolar II/other.
doctor.question: Looking back at that time when you felt so energetic and wired, did that period ever last for a full week or longer?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the duration of the hypomanic/manic episode (whether it lasted a full week or longer). The symptom profile contains 'duration' (which refers to the current depressive episode - 2 weeks) and 'depressive_episode_duration' (1 year), but it does not contain a specific duration for the elevated/increased energy episode.

patient.answer: No, it didn't last that long. It was just a few days, maybe four or five at the most, where I felt like that. It definitely wasn't a whole week.

inference.note: The patient confirmed that the elevated mood period lasted only a few days (less than a week) and did not require hospitalization, which supports a hypomanic episode (ruling out F31.1/Manic episode). Given the history of depressive symptoms meeting criteria for a major depressive episode and the presence of a hypomanic episode, F31.0 (Bipolar disorder, current episode hypomanic) is the appropriate fit as the patient is currently experiencing a depressive episode following a prior hypomanic episode.
